A 25-year-old male marathon runner with no significant past medical history presents to the clinic with
low back pain. The patient reports a dull, constant low back pain that began 2 weeks ago after lifting
furniture. The pain is relieved when he lies down and worsens if he sits or stands for prolonged periods
of time. On osteopathic structural examination, there is tenderness to palpation in the musculature of
the lumbar region. The physician places their thumbs on the transverse processes of L3 and notes their
right thumb appears more posterior than the left, but this resolves when the patient arches his spine. If
this patient were treated with high-velocity/low-amplitude technique, the correct setup would be Answer
Choices: (A) Patient right lateral recumbent, left foot hooks into the right popliteal fossa, torso rotated
toward the ground (B) Patient right lateral recumbent, right foot hooks into the left popliteal fossa, torso
rotated toward the ceiling (C) Patient right lateral recumbent, right lower extremity hangs off the table,
torso rotated toward the ceiling (D) Patient left lateral recumbent, left foot hooks into the right popliteal
fossa, torso rotated toward the ground (E) Patient left lateral recumbent, left lower extremity hangs off
the table, torso rotated toward the ground (F) Patient right lateral recumbent, left lower extremity hangs
over the treatment table, torso rotated toward the ground (G) Patient left lateral recumbent, right lower
extremity hangs over the treatment table, torso rotated toward the ceiling (H) Patient left lateral
recumbent, right foot hooks into the left popliteal fossa, torso rotated toward the ceiling (I) Patient left
lateral recumbent, left foot hooks into the right popliteal fossa, torso rotated toward the ceiling (J)
